Recent advances in transfer printing

Abstract 
The evolution of human–machine interfaces (HMI) toward more immersive and intuitive forms, such as wearable 
devices and augmented reality systems, demands the development of high-performance flexible electronics. Het-
erogeneous integration, which combines diverse inorganic materials and functional devices onto unconventional 
substrates, is the core strategy for realizing these next-generation systems. The success of this approach, however, 
critically hinges on the ability to precisely transfer and assemble vast quantities of micro-scale components. This paper 
reviews the state-of-the-art in inorganic thin-film transfer technologies, which are the essential enablers for this para-
digm shift. We systematically categorize and discuss the mechanisms, advantages, and drawbacks of three primary 
approaches: physical, chemical, and self-assembly transfer methods. Furthermore, we introduce recent applications 
of semiconductor devices developed via these techniques. The continued advancement of these transfer technolo-
gies is poised to catalyze transformative innovations in how users interact with the digital world, fundamentally 
reshaping applications in medicine, personal computing, and beyond.
Keywords  Inorganic thin-film, Thin-film transfer, Heterogeneous integration, Flexible semiconductor systems
Introduction
The paradigm of human–machine interfaces (HMI) 
is undergoing a fundamental transformation, moving 
beyond rigid, two-dimensional screens toward systems 
that are conformally integrated with the human body and 
surrounding environments [1–5]. This evolution is driven 
by the broader trends of the fourth industrial revolu-
tion, where new digital technologies are fundamentally 
reshaping society, industry, and the economy. A core 
component of this transformation is the internet of things 
(IoT), which necessitates active and seamless information 
exchange between users, devices, and the environment. 
To meet these demands, a key challenge is form factor 
innovation, the strategic redesign of electronic devices 
to enhance their utility, portability, and user experi-
ence, ultimately aiming to seamlessly merge the digital 
and physical worlds. This has led to a surge in research 
focused on transforming high-performance, stable, and 
durable electronic devices into flexible and wearable for-
mats [6–11].
Among these innovations, flexible displays are 
emerging as a critical medium for delivering visual 
information in next-generation HMIs [12–19]. Visual 
information accounts for the vast majority of human 
perception, and flexible displays enable its integra-
tion onto diverse surfaces like vehicle interiors, build-
ings, and clothing [20–23]. This technology is pivotal

immersive systems like virtual reality (VR) and aug-

autonomous driving, medicine, and education [24–27]. 
To achieve the demanding performance required for 
these next-generation displays, micro light-emitting 
diodes (μLEDs) have become a leading candidate 
[28–32]. These ultra-small (width < 100  μm, thick-
ness < 5  μm) and ultra-thin devices offer exceptional 
characteristics, including high resolution (> 5,000 PPI), 
outstanding brightness (> 100,000  cd/m2), low power 
consumption (< 40 mW), and rapid response times 
(~ 0.2 ns). However, a significant hurdle is that μLEDs 
are inherently monochromatic. To create a full-color 
display, red, green, and blue μLEDs, which are fabri-
cated on different native substrates, must be precisely 
transferred and integrated onto a single final substrate 
[33–35]. This fundamental requirement has spurred 
significant research into heterogeneous integration, 
a field dedicated to combining diverse materials and 
devices on a common platform to achieve novel func-
tionalities [36–42]. The success of creating advanced 
HMIs is therefore entirely dependent on the existence 
of robust and high-yield thin-film transfer processes 
[43, 44]. For commercial viability, these processes must 
be fast, scalable for mass production, and allow for the 
reuse of expensive donor substrates [45–47]. However, 
significant challenges remain in transferring massive 
quantities of micro-scale devices with the required 
speed and precision [48–50]. For instance, assembling 
a single flexible μLED display composed of tens of 
millions of pixels could require over 100,000 transfer 
steps, a process that could take more than a day even 
if one hundred devices are transferred simultaneously.
This paper provides a comprehensive review of the 
inorganic thin-film transfer processes that are the core 
enabling technologies for these heterogeneously inte-
grated flexible semiconductor systems. These pro-
cesses are essential for moving materials and devices 
from their rigid growth substrates to the final flexible, 
stretchable, or wearable substrates that will form the 
foundation of future HMIs. We broadly classify and 
analyze these techniques in three main categories: 
(i) physical transfer, (ii) chemical transfer, and (iii) 
self-assembly-based transfer. In the following sec-
tions, we will detail the mechanisms, advantages, and 
disadvantages of each method and introduce recent 
application studies of semiconductor devices realized 
through these innovative transfer technologies, includ-
ing displays, batteries, memories, and wearable devices 
(Fig. 1).
Inorganic thin film transfer methods
The inorganic thin-film transfer technologies for imple-
menting heterogeneously integrated flexible semiconduc-
tor systems can be broadly divided into three categories 
based on the core principle used to release and relocate 
devices. These are physical transfer, which directly uti-
lizes physical forces; chemical transfer, which separates 
devices through specific chemical reactions; and self-
assembly transfer, which guides numerous devices to 
align themselves through external driving forces. Each 
approach possesses unique advantages and disadvan-
tages, and the appropriate technique is selected based on 
the type, scale, and precision requirements of the target 
device.
Physical transfer
Physical transfer methods use physical forces (e.g., 
mechanical, thermal, and electrical) to detach semicon-
ductor devices from a donor substrate and move them 
to a new target substrate. A fundamental example is the 
stamping method, which uses the adhesive force of a pol-
ymer elastomer stamp to pick up and place micro-scale 
devices, thereby creating flexible, stretchable, or wearable 
systems [51–59]. As illustrated in Fig. 2a, one advanced 
physical transfer method, known as cilia-assisted trans-
fer printing, uniquely addresses the challenge of applying 
electronic devices to complex and uneven surfaces like 
textiles [60]. An advanced physical transfer method, cilia-
assisted transfer printing, is uniquely suited for apply-
ing devices to complex and uneven surfaces like textiles. 
This technique uses microscopic, hair-like structures 
(artificial cilia) fabricated on the device periphery. These 
cilia provide robust adhesion by mechanically wrapping 
around target fibers and also serve as stress dampers, 
protecting the device during mechanical deformation. 
Using this approach, high-performance inorganic semi-
conductor devices, such as indium gallium zinc oxide 
(IGZO)-based transistors and 7-stage ring oscillator cir-
cuits, have been successfully transferred onto wearable 
textiles. The cilia serve a dual purpose, also functioning 
as effective stress dampers that protect the electronic 
device performance during mechanical deformation. 
This results in remarkable durability, with the transferred 
IGZO circuits maintaining stable operation even after 
10,000 cycles of stretching and release, as well as daily 
wearing and washing. The versatility of this technique 
has been demonstrated by transferring devices of various 
shapes and sizes, ranging from 300 × 300 µm to 1 × 1 cm, 
onto diverse, non-ideal surfaces including bandages, tea 
strainers, and even stones. The primary advantages of 
this technology are its relatively low cost and the dura-
bility of the stamps, which allows for repetitive transfer

To address the throughput limitations of planar stamp-
ing, roll-based processing was developed to enable 
continuous, large-scale manufacturing. To address the 
throughput limitations of stamping, roll-based process-
ing was developed for continuous manufacturing. An 
advanced version is the high-speed, high-temperature 
shear-rolling process, which achieves unidirectional 
alignment of a block copolymer (BCP)-based nanopat-
terns in approximately 0.1  s at up to 280  °C (Fig.  2b). 
A key innovation is the use of a polydimethylsiloxane 
(PDMS) pad with a nano-bumpy surface, which mini-
mizes friction and compressive stress to prevent film 
damage at such high temperatures [61–65]. This coun-
terintuitively minimizes unwanted friction and compres-
sive stress, allowing for effective and uniform shearing. 
This method can create highly ordered line-space pat-
terns with a half-pitch as small as 8  nm. Furthermore, 
its potential for mass production has been validated by 
successfully applying it to long, 3-inch wide flexible poly-
imide films, demonstrating its suitability for future roll-
to-roll manufacturing systems. While this enhancement 
in mass-production capability can significantly reduce 
process time and costs, the technique inherits the pri-
mary drawback of stamp-based methods: any deforma-
tion in the polymer composite material can lead to poor 
transfer precision, necessitating further improvements.
Laser transfer, also known as laser lift-off (LLO), is a 
process technology that utilizes a high-energy laser beam 
to induce a reaction in a sacrificial layer on the donor 
substrate, leading to the separation of the semiconduc-
tor device, as depicted in Fig. 2c [66–71]. A prime exam-
ple is the transfer of high-performance, skin-like indium 
zinc oxide (IZO) thin-film transistors (TFTs) for flexible 
transparent displays. The process begins with the growth 
of a laser-reactive sacrificial layer, such as hydrogenated

through the transparent substrate. This laser irradiation

reduces the interfacial adhesive force, allowing the entire 
upper device layer to be cleanly detached from the donor 
substrate and transferred to a new flexible substrate, 
such as an ultrathin (4  µm) PET film. This technology 
offers several advantages, including the ability to transfer 
high-performance devices without significant degrada-
tion (e.g., mobility of ~ 40 ­cm2V−1 ­s−1 and transparency 
of > 83% for IZO TFTs) and the potential for reusing the 
expensive donor substrate. However, its disadvantages 
include the requirement for expensive laser equipment 
and the constraint that the process is only applicable to 
transparent substrates [72–81]. While the laser can leave 
behind an unclean surface on the donor substrate (e.g., 
agglomerated Si nanostructures), this residue can typi-
cally be removed through subsequent etching processes.
Electrostatic transfer utilizes an array of microscopic 
transfer heads to selectively pick up and place micro-
devices using a controlled voltage (Fig.  2d). As devel-
oped by LuxVue, this method generates an electrostatic 
attraction force to lift devices and an electrostatic repul-
sive force to release them, enabling precise, array-based 
assembly suitable for display manufacturing. However, 
the transfer heads are based on complex and expensive 
micro-electro-mechanical systems (MEMS) technology, 
and care must be taken to prevent device damage from 
electrostatic discharge (ESD) [82–87].
Electromagnetic transfer relies on a programmable 
magnetic module to attract a ferromagnetic layer (e.g., 
Ni) temporarily deposited on the micro-devices. This 
non-contact approach minimizes mechanical damage, 
allowing for precise and selective transfer, as shown in 
Fig. 2e [83]. The main challenges are the manufacturing 
complexity of the programmable magnetic modules and 
the necessity of a multi-step process that includes the 
deposition and subsequent removal of the ferromagnetic 
layer.

using laser-induced etching (LIE), a technology that cre-

A novel, large-area approach is 2D material-based 
layer transfer (2DLT), which enables wafer-scale thin 
film transfer using primarily mechanical force [89–92]. 
The process, depicted in Fig. 3b, begins with the coating 
of a two-dimensional material, such as graphene, onto a 
donor substrate [93]. The desired semiconductor material 
is then grown on top of this 2D layer via a process known 
as remote epitaxy. This unique growth method allows 
the single-crystal structure of the underlying donor 
wafer to be copied through the atomically thin graphene, 
resulting in a high-quality, single-crystal semiconductor 
film that is only weakly bonded to the substrate by van 
der Waals forces. This weak interface allows the newly 
grown film to be easily exfoliated from the donor sub-
strate, often initiated by depositing a high-stress metal 
layer, typically Ni, to induce delamination. This technol-
ogy has been successfully utilized to create freestanding, 
ultrathin (200  nm) single-crystalline GaN membranes 
for advanced applications like chip-less wireless elec-
tronic skins (e-skins). Characterization of these trans-
ferred GaN films using high-resolution X-ray diffraction 
(HRXRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) 
has confirmed their perfect single-crystallinity and ori-
ented atomic planes, which are essential for high-perfor-
mance devices. Due to their atomically thin nature, 2D 
materials facilitate the growth of these high-performance 
semiconductors while circumventing the lattice mis-
match issues common in conventional heteroepitaxy. The 
2DLT technology offers significant advantages, including 
the ability to reuse the donor substrate without damage, 
a reduction in material and process costs, and the crea-
tion of freestanding films far thinner than what can be 
achieved by mechanical polishing. This makes it a pow-
erful platform for fabricating next-generation flexible and 
wearable electronics.

Chemical transfer
Chemical transfer methods are defined by the use of a 
specific chemical solution to selectively remove a sacri-
ficial layer or substrate. This process releases pre-fabri-
cated devices from their donor substrate, making them 
free-standing and ready for transfer. The key principle is 
the controlled dissolution of an intermediate layer, which 
distinguishes it from other transfer approaches. The pri-
mary technique in this category is epitaxial lift-off (ELO), 
a transfer technology that selectively etches only a sacri-
ficial layer located between the donor substrate and the 
device to achieve separation [95, 96]. For instance, ELO 
has been used to transfer a ferromagnetic ­La0.7Sr0.3MnO3 
(LSMO) film by first growing it on an ideal ­SrTiO3 (STO) 
substrate with an intermediate sacrificial layer of ­SrRuO3 
(SRO). The entire structure is then immersed in a ­NaIO4 
aqueous solution, which selectively dissolves the SRO 
layer over several hours, allowing the high-quality LSMO 
film to be released (Fig. 4a) [97]. This technology is con-
siderably simpler than most physical transfer processes 
and does not require expensive laser or electrical module 
equipment, offering the advantage of low-cost transfer 
through simple chemical treatment. A significant ben-
efit of ELO is that it allows for the growth of films on 
ideal, lattice-matched substrates, avoiding the defects 
and performance degradation that occur when growing 
directly on an incompatible final substrate. In the case of 
the LSMO film, this strain-release via ELO led to a 19% 
increase in its saturation magnetization. Furthermore, 
cross-sectional scanning TEM (STEM) was utilized to 
verify that the exfoliated device layer was successfully 
transferred with a well-defined interface, as shown in 
Fig. 4b. However, this process technology suffers from a 
very slow process speed due to the long diffusion times 
required for the etchant. The use of chemical etchants 
can also lead to challenges, such as the formation of 
unintended residues at the transfer interface and poten-
tial degradation of the donor substrate surface, which can 
affect its reusability [98–100].
An enhancement to this method involves actively 
engineering stress within the film to accelerate the lift-
off process, a technique known as internal stressor-
enhanced ELO (i-ELO). While still leveraging interfacial 
forces, this advanced approach embeds an internal sac-
rificial stressor layer (ISSL) within the device epitaxial 
structure [101]. For example, in GaAs solar cell fabrica-
tion, quantum well-like GaInAs layers are intentionally 
grown inside the device stack. These layers have a differ-
ent lattice constant from GaAs, introducing a controlled 
compressive strain. When the AlAs sacrificial layer is 
exposed to an etchant, typically a mixture of HF and ace-
tone, this built-in strain induces a strong self-rollup force, 
actively peeling the film upward, as displayed in Fig. 4c. 
This action creates a wider channel for fresh etchant to 
access the sacrificial layer, dramatically increasing the 
etch rate. In addition to the internal stressor, a polyme-
thyl methacrylate (PMMA) polymer layer is often coated 
on the surface, acting not only as a mechanical support 
but also as an external stressor that swells in the etch-
ant to further control the film curvature. This combined 
effect of internal and external stressors was shown to 
increase the lateral etching rate by approximately 5 times 
compared to conventional methods (Fig. 4d). This highly 
controllable and rapid self-peeling mechanism signifi-
cantly improves throughput and reliability, making it a

Self‑assembly transfer
In contrast to methods that transfer pre-arranged arrays, 
self-assembly transfer involves the spontaneous and 
parallel alignment and bonding of a massive number of 
micro-devices that are initially dispersed randomly in a 
liquid. Driven by external forces such as fluid dynamics, 
magnetic, or electric fields, these devices independently 
find and secure themselves onto designated receptor 
sites on a target substrate. One prominent technique 
is fluidic self-assembly (FSA) [106, 107]. Traditionally, 
FSA has struggled with sub-100 µm devices due to their 
low inertia, which leads to poor assembly yields (< 5%). 
However, a recent breakthrough demonstrated that this 
challenge can be overcome by controlling the fluid vis-
cosity. By adding a small amount of poloxamer poly-
mer to the assembly solution, its viscosity is moderately 
increased. This enhanced viscosity significantly improves 
the momentum transfer from the agitated liquid to the 
micro-devices, providing them with enough force to 
overcome fluid resistance and form a stable bond at the 
target site. As shown in Fig. 5a, pre-processing steps are 
performed on both the device chiplets and the receiver 
substrate to ensure accurate transfer [108]. For instance,

of the binding sites and chiplet contact pads to ensure a 
precise one-to-one assembly.
An alternative approach is electric field self-assembly 
transfer, which has evolved into advanced hybrid meth-
ods that combine multiple physical forces for enhanced 
efficiency and precision. A prominent example is the 
MDSAT (Magnetic-force-assisted Dielectrophoretic Self-
Assembly Technology), which leverages both long-range 
magnetic force for transport and short-range dielectro-
phoretic (DEP) force for precise capture and alignment 
[109]. In this technology, micro-scale semiconductor 
devices, such as RGB µLEDs, are designed to include a 
ferromagnetic material within their structure. The assem-
bly process, schematically shown in Fig. 5c, begins with 
dispersing these µLEDs in a fluid-filled chamber contain-
ing the target substrate. An array of rotating magnets 
moves beneath the substrate, generating a long-range 
magnetic force that gathers the µLEDs into a cluster and 
sweeps them across the entire substrate surface, ensur-
ing they are delivered near the target sites. Once a µLED 
approaches a designated receptor hole on the substrate, 
a highly localized, non-uniform electric field generates a 
powerful, short-range DEP force. As simulated in Fig. 5d, 
this DEP force is approximately 10 times stronger than 
the magnetic force within the immediate vicinity of the 
receptor, enabling it to overcome the magnetic transport 
force and firmly capture the µLED in its precise location. 
This dual-force method allows for the concurrent self-
assembly of RGB µLEDs in a single step through shape 
matching, where different colored LEDs have unique 
shapes that fit only into correspondingly shaped recep-
tor holes. This technology demonstrates extremely high 
throughput and precision, achieving a simultaneous RGB 
transfer yield of 99.99% within 15 min. It is also highly 
scalable for large-area substrates, making it a strong can-
didate for mass production. However, it requires a more 
complex device structure with embedded ferromagnetic 
materials and a sophisticated substrate design with inte-
grated assembly electrodes, and care must still be taken 
to avoid potential device degradation from the applied 
fields.
Application fields of transfer technology
Wearable device
The development of the high-performance inorganic 
thin-film transfer processes described above has cata-
lyzed the rapid global advancement of semiconduc-
tor and electronic devices with innovative form factors, 
including flexible, stretchable, and even wearable sys-
tems.[110–115] In particular, the ability to transfer and 
integrate heterogeneous thin-film materials and devices 
onto a single substrate has enabled the incorporation of 
diverse functions within a single system. This has led to 
innovative breakthroughs in next-generation electronic 
applications, such as medical wearable devices, flexible 
thin-film batteries, transistors, memories, and displays.
[116–121]
Wearable devices have demonstrated significant 
potential for various medical applications, ranging from 
monitoring a user health status to providing personal-

designed for advanced optogenetics.[129] Its fabrica-

high-purity GaN LED layers from their rigid growth 
wafer. This crucial step allows high-performance 
inorganic films to be integrated onto a flexible, body-
conformable substrate. This LLO step allows for the 
transfer of high-performance, high-temperature pro-
cessed GaN thin films onto a temporary carrier, which 
is a key enabler for creating flexible devices. Following 
this initial transfer, a simple monolithic fabrication pro-

Energy device
Power sources are an indispensable component of any 
semiconductor system. Among various power devices, 
lithium-ion batteries have traditionally been difficult to 
render in a flexible format, posing a challenge for their 
application in flexible and wearable electronic systems 
[130–137]. A primary reason is that high-performance 
inorganic electrode materials, such as crystalline lithium 
cobalt oxide ­(LiCoO2), require high-temperature anneal-
ing (typically around 700°C) to achieve optimal perfor-
mance, a process that would melt or degrade polymer 
substrates. To overcome this, a physical transfer method 
based on mechanical peeling has been developed, as dis-
cussed in the context of stamping-based approaches in 
Sect. "Physical Transfer". As shown in Fig. 6c, a complete, 
high-performance battery is fabricated on a rigid mica 
substrate, which has an intrinsically weak layered struc-
ture. This allows the entire battery stack to be cleanly 
delaminated and transferred to a flexible substrate with-
out damage [138]. This mechanical transfer is achieved 
simply by peeling off the battery film using the adhesive 
force of a commercial tape (e.g., 3M Scotch tape) without 
damaging the device. The freestanding thin-film battery 
is then transferred to a final flexible substrate like PDMS 
and encapsulated. The resulting high-performance flex-
ible lithium-ion battery was able to maintain a high 
energy density of 2.2 × ­103 μWh/cm3 and a current den-
sity of 46.5 μA/cm2 even in a bent state. The long-term 
reliability of this flexible battery was also confirmed. As 
demonstrated in the charge/discharge curves of Fig. 6d, 
even after 100 cycles, the battery exhibited excellent 
capacity retention. This stable performance was main-
tained not only in a flat state but also when severely bent 
to a radius of 3.1 mm, proving the outstanding mechani-
cal and electrochemical robustness of the device created 
by this transfer process and suggesting a significant con-
tribution to the development of fully flexible electronic 
systems.
Electronics
To implement next-generation flexible systems through 
heterogeneous integration, high-performance logic and 
driving circuits that can stably operate various compo-
nents are essential [139, 140]. The driving method pre-
dominantly used in the display field is the active matrix 
(AM) method, which is typically composed of thin-film 
transistors (TFTs) and capacitors. In this architecture, 
the capacitors provide a constant current to each pixel, 
while the TFTs serve as switching devices to drive only 
the desired elements, making high-performance TFTs 
essential for rendering the desired images and controlling 
the system. Figure 6e shows a high-performance, single-
crystal Si TFT array fabricated through a load-controlled 
roll-based stamp transfer process. This automated physi-
cal transfer technique, an advanced form of the stamping 
methods described in Sect. "Physical Transfer", enables 
the large-area integration of high-performance circuits 
onto flexible substrates [141]. Among various semi-
conductor materials for TFTs, single-crystal Si is par-
ticularly suitable due to its compatibility with   existing 
CMOS processes, relatively low cost, and excellent elec-
trical characteristics (mobility: ~750  ­cm2/Vs). The pro-
cess begins with fabricating Si TFT arrays connected by 
anchors on a silicon-on-insulator (SOI) substrate. These 
arrays are then made free-standing by selectively etch-
ing and removing the lower SiO layer. A key part of this 
transfer process is the use of a roll-type PDMS stamp 
equipped with a feedback module containing load sen-
sors and z-axis actuators. This system precisely controls 
the size and uniformity of the contact load during the 
roll transfer. The roller with the PDMS stamp moves over 
the freestanding Si TFT array, peeling the devices off the 
donor substrate. The array is then transferred to a final 
serpentine-structured plastic substrate with fine align-
ment. As demonstrated in Fig. 6f of the referenced paper, 
devices transferred via this method maintain remark-
ably stable performance even when subjected to various 
bending radii, showing negligible changes in their driving 
voltage, which confirms the excellent mechanical reliabil-
ity of the process. This automated roll-transfer technique 
allows for the precise, high-yield integration of high-
performance Si-based circuits onto flexible platforms, 
providing the essential backplane for driving complex 
heterogeneously integrated systems.
Memory, a storage device that retains data as electrical 
signals, is another indispensable component in electronic 
systems. Among emerging next-generation memory 
technologies, resistive random-access memory (RRAM) 
is notable for its fast response, low power consumption, 
and high durability. However, fabricating high-perfor-
mance inorganic RRAM directly on polymer substrates 
is challenging because the required high-temperature

which integrates a selector diode with each RRAM cell,

flexible 1S-1R arrays remained stable without peeling or 
cracking, demonstrating that the LLO transfer process 
enables the realization of high-performance, high-density 
flexible memory devices with excellent mechanical stabil-
ity and functionality.
Display
High-resolution displays, which are attracting significant 
attention as candidates for next-generation electronic 
devices, can be manufactured using µLEDs to meet the 
extreme demands of AR/VR [143–147]. While conven-
tional displays rely on the lateral, side-by-side arrange-
ment of RGB pixels, this approach fundamentally limits 
the achievable pixel density. To overcome this, research 
is being conducted to implement vertically stacked RGB 
µLEDs, where the different color subpixels are layered 
on top of each other, allowing for a dramatic increase in 
resolution from a single pixel area [148]. The key ena-
bling technology for this vertical integration is the 2D 
material-based layer transfer (2DLT) process, a mechani-
cal exfoliation-based physical transfer method discussed 
in Sect. "Physical Transfer". This method utilizes the 
weak van der Waals forces between a 2D material (like 
graphene) and an epitaxially grown semiconductor film, 
allowing the film to be easily and cleanly peeled off and 
stacked vertically. The separated, ultrathin R, G, and B 
LED membranes are then sequentially transferred and 
stacked using adhesive polymer interlayers, achieving 
semiconductor heterogeneous integration, as displayed 
in Fig. 6i. This 2DLT approach has led to a breakthrough 
in display technology, enabling the fabrication of the 
world’s smallest vertical µLEDs with a lateral size of just 
4 µm and a total stack height of only 9 µm. This achieve-
ment overcomes the high-aspect-ratio fabrication chal-
lenges of previous vertical stacking methods and has 
resulted in a record-breaking array density of 5100 PPI 
(Fig. 6j). These devices provide a high luminance in the 
range of ­104–106 cd/m2, which is more than sufficient for 
AR/VR applications that require clear and vivid images. 
This technological development, combining epitaxy and 
layer transfer, is a crucial step toward manufacturing the 
ultra-high-resolution displays that will define the future 
of immersive user interfaces.
Perspective and conclusion
The heterogeneous integration and associated transfer 
technologies reviewed in this paper play a central and 
indispensable role in the development of next-generation 
electronic devices. By enabling the integration of diverse, 
high-performance materials and devices onto flexible and 
wearable substrates, these technologies provide a foun-
dation for surpassing the performance limits of conven-
tional electronics and creating novel functionalities and 
application paradigms. The impact of these advance-
ments is already evident across various application 
fields. In biomedical engineering, flexible µLED devices 
implemented through LLO processes have shown their 
potential as minimally invasive tools for brain stimula-
tion in optogenetics, achieving high optical performance 
of ~30 mW/mm2 at a thickness of only 15 µm. Similarly, 
high-performance flexible lithium-ion batteries and 
silicon TFTs have been successfully transferred to flex-
ible substrates via mechanical peeling and roll transfer, 
respectively, enabling the creation of fully integrated flex-
ible systems. These successful demonstrations underscore 
that inorganic thin-film transfer processes are poised to 
greatly contribute to the advancement of various port-
able electronic devices. Notably, 2DLT has opened a new 
path for manufacturing high-resolution AR/VR displays 
by enabling vertically stacked µLEDs, achieving a record-
breaking resolution of 5100 PPI. Despite this progress, 
significant challenges must be addressed before these 
technologies can be widely commercialized. Key issues 
include minimizing mechanical damage to micro-scale 
device chips during transfer, the need for improved align-
ment precision, and the development of cost-effective 
methods for donor substrate reuse. Furthermore, the 
transfer process itself can significantly affect device prop-
erties. For example, the electrical and optical characteris-
tics of GaN µLEDs can change depending on the transfer 
temperature, necessitating methods to analyze and opti-
mize these effects on device performance. Securing mate-
rial compatibility between the transferred device and the 
final substrate, as well as developing process plans to cor-
rect or repair incorrectly transferred devices, also remain 
critical areas of development. Prospectively, heterogene-
ous integration is positioned as a linchpin technology, 
essential for transcending the performance boundaries

Abstract: The evolution of human–machine interfaces (HMI) toward more immersive and intuitive forms, such as wearable devices and augmented reality systems, demands the development of high-performance flexible electronics. Het- erogeneous integration, which combines diverse inorganic materials and functional devices onto unconventional substrates, is the core strategy for realizing these next-generation systems. The success of this approach, however, critically hinges on the ability to precisely transfer and assemble vast quantities of micro-scale components. This paper reviews the state-of-the-art in inorganic thin-film transfer technologies, which are the essential enablers for this para- digm shift. We systematically categorize and discuss the mechanisms, advantages, and drawbacks of three primary approaches: physical, chemical, and self-assembly transfer methods. Furthermore, we introduce recent applications of semiconductor devices developed via these techniques. The continued advancement of these transfer technolo- gies is poised to catalyze transformative innovations in how users interact with the digital world, fundamentally reshaping applications in medicine, personal computing, and beyond.
